newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia launches digital satellite TV service.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia launches digital satellite TV service.

text.p: Malaysia launched a digital satellite television and radio service on Wednesday billed as the most advanced in Asia and aimed at promoting the country as a regional broadcasting hub.

MEASAT Broadcast announced at a glitzy launch ceremony that it will start delivering 22 digital television channels of laser disc quality and eight radio channels with compact disc quality sound to Malaysian consumers starting next month.
"It will be the most advanced television system in Asia," MEASAT's chief operating officer Paul Edwards said.

Viewers will receive the service under the "Astro" brandname via a 60-centimetre (two feet) dish -- the first of its kind in Asia. The decoder and receiver for the dish will also have a hard disc to provide multimedia capabilities including Internet access, home banking and shopping, Edwards said.

Speaking at the launch, Information Minister Mohamad Rahmat said the government will introduce amendments to the Broadcast Act in parliament next month to legalise the use of parabolic dishes and decoders.
The amendments will only allow the use of 60 centimetre dishes which can receive signals solely from the MEASAT satellite.
"Inevitably, we will open our sky, but just a little, with the use of a specific satellite dish approved by the ministry," Mohamed said.
Malaysia had banned the use of parabolic dishes to keep its airwaves clear of sex and violence -- and, diplomats said, unflattering news programmes, as well.
MEASAT -- 85 percent owned by telecommunications company Binariang Sdn Bhd and 15 percent by the Ministry of Finance -- launched Malaysia's first communications satellite in January.

It plans to launch a second one next year and another in 1998. The third satellite will be much bigger than the first two and have the capacity to deliver hundreds of channels to niche markets around the world, Edwards said.
MEASAT will initially be sold to Malaysian consumers. But by mid-year 1997 it hopes to sell it to other countries in its footprint -- India, Indonesia, Taiwan, the Philippines and eastern Australia.

They will receive Malay, Chinese and Tamil language channels -- the three main ethnic groups in Malaysia and among the major languages of Asia. Hong Kong's TVB will supply programmes for the Chinese channel and India's state-run Doordarshan will provide Indian-language programming.
News channels include CNN International, U.S. network NBC, its business channel CNBC, and Dow Jones' Asia Business News.

The rest will be devoted to sports and entertainment, including Star Sports, the ESPN sports network, Home Box Office, Star Movies, MGM Gold, the Disney Channel, Star Plus, the Cartoon Network and the documentary channel, Discovery.

MEASAT will produce its own programming as well at its 350,000 square foot "All-Asia Broadcast Centre", which the company describes as "the world's largest all-digital broadcast and production centre".
The centre is the first to locate in the newly-launched "multimedia super corridor", a 15- by 50-km zone south of Kuala Lumpur aimed at attracting world-class information technology companies.
Installation costs for the system were put at 1,500 ringgit ($600) with a monthly subscription of 80 ringgit ($32).
